name: Business Analyst Blair
summary: Blair turns service needs, policy constraints and accessibility expectations into verifiable requirements and handoffs.
scenario: Blair supports a government digital-service team replacing a complex application form. The procurement and delivery teams want concise requirements, accountable handoffs and observable acceptance evidence.
goals: Write accessibility requirements that can be verified rather than relying on generic compliance claims. | Map each delivery decision to a responsible role without treating ARRM as an organizational mandate. | Find the right W3C source to cite in an acceptance criterion.
needs: Examples of requirements, acceptance evidence and handoff language. | A clear distinction between normative WCAG requirements and advisory ARRM task assignments. | Traceability from a requirement to its WCAG criterion and relevant ARRM task.
thoughts: Who needs to make this decision, and where should it be recorded? | What evidence would establish that the delivered interaction works?
feelings: Concerned when accessibility is reduced to an untestable statement in a contract. | More confident when requirements, owners and review evidence are visible together.
behaviors: Cross-references requirements, issue tickets and design decisions. | Reviews procurement or acceptance documents with content, design, QA and development colleagues.
pain_points: Vague wording such as fully accessible with no observable acceptance criteria. | A list of technical failures without a clear consequence for scope, delivery or verification.
access_context: May need to review evidence in a managed browser without installing local tools; this is a situational constraint, not a property of all business analysts.
communication_framing: Lead with the decision or expected outcome, then show a verifiable example and responsible collaborators.
preferred_vocabulary: requirement | acceptance criterion | risk | scope | decision | evidence | traceability
example_types: acceptance criterion | procurement requirement | handoff decision | risk register entry
success_signal: Can explain which requirement is normative, which task is advisory, and what evidence would help check the outcome.
avatar_attribution: RoboHash (https://robohash.org/), classic robot artwork by Zikri Kader

name: Content Author Casey
summary: Casey maintains content across a large site and needs guidance that makes accessible publishing practical and repeatable.
scenario: Casey edits guidance pages, images, form instructions and documents in a CMS. They coordinate with designers and developers but cannot change underlying component code.
goals: Write labels, link text, headings and text alternatives that convey their intended meaning. | Apply repeatable editorial checks to new and existing content. | Know when content needs a design or code change instead of another editorial revision.
needs: Before-and-after writing examples with context. | Plain-language explanations of source criteria and role assignments. | A checklist for checking published content, including surrounding context.
thoughts: What does someone need to understand or do after reading this? | Is the problem in the words, the content structure or the component itself?
feelings: Frustrated by advice that assumes a content editor can edit HTML templates. | Reassured by examples that distinguish an authoring decision from a developer handoff.
behaviors: Uses a CMS preview and checks published pages against source material. | Collaborates on alt text, error messages and content patterns.
pain_points: Guidance that gives only a success-criterion number and no editorial example. | A CMS that makes the right authoring choice difficult or impossible.
access_context: Sometimes reviews material at high browser zoom when checking readability and content structure; this is an example context, not an assumption about content professionals.
communication_framing: Start with what the reader needs to understand; show a concrete content example and when to ask others for help.
preferred_vocabulary: reader | purpose | meaning | label | heading | alternative text | publishing workflow
example_types: link rewrite | image alternative | heading outline | form-instruction edit
success_signal: Can make or request the correct editorial change and inspect it in its published context.
avatar_attribution: RoboHash (https://robohash.org/), classic robot artwork by Zikri Kader

name: Front-End Developer Finley
summary: Finley implements accessible components and wants precise, testable guidance tied to browser behavior and W3C references.
scenario: Finley maintains a reusable component library in an open-source web project. They fix defects in keyboard behavior, names, roles, states, focus and responsive rendering.
goals: Translate an assigned task into robust semantics and predictable browser behavior. | Verify a change using automated checks plus manual keyboard and assistive-technology testing. | Preserve design and content decisions while implementing accessible interaction.
needs: Short technical examples, valid HTML and clear failure cases. | Reproducible browser and assistive-technology test steps. | Direct links to W3C criteria and the precise ARRM task and collaborator.
thoughts: What browser behavior must change, and how can I reproduce the failure? | Is this problem caused by markup, CSS, scripting, authoring content or interaction design?
feelings: Frustrated by vague accessibility guidance with no concrete failure mode. | More confident when expected behavior and a reproducible test are recorded.
behaviors: Works from issues and pull requests with repeatable test cases. | Checks dynamic states using keyboard, browser tools and assistive technology.
pain_points: A design handoff without keyboard, focus or error states. | Automated test scores being treated as sufficient proof of accessibility.
access_context: May work on locked-down or remote development systems and need implementation advice that does not depend on one proprietary tool.
communication_framing: Start with an observable failure and expected behavior; provide implementation detail, test procedure and the source criterion.
preferred_vocabulary: semantic HTML | CSS | JavaScript | keyboard behavior | accessible name | component | test case
example_types: HTML example | component behavior contract | Playwright fixture | keyboard test case
success_signal: Can implement the change and explain which parts remain subject to manual testing and team review.
avatar_attribution: RoboHash (https://robohash.org/), classic robot artwork by Zikri Kader

name: UX Designer Uma
summary: Uma designs user journeys and prototypes, checking whether people can complete important interactions across different access needs.
scenario: Uma maps an online service journey, including authentication, error recovery and support. Stakeholders frequently mistake a working prototype for evidence that the final experience is accessible.
goals: Identify barriers in user flows before implementation. | Connect interaction decisions to user needs and evaluation scenarios. | Make handoffs between research, content, visual design and development explicit.
needs: User journey and interaction examples linked to criteria. | Examples of task failures, alternative paths and recovery states. | Questions suitable for moderated and assistive-technology usability research.
thoughts: What happens when someone cannot complete this step as designed? | How do we know the proposed interaction actually supports the task?
feelings: Concerned when a polished prototype obscures untested interaction states. | More confident after hearing evidence from participants with varied access needs.
behaviors: Develops journey maps, task flows, prototypes and research scripts. | Revises designs after observing where people get stuck.
pain_points: Conformance labels with little description of user impact. | Missing states for errors, timeouts, keyboard navigation and interrupted journeys.
access_context: Often presents prototypes remotely, where participants may have different devices, connection quality and assistive technologies.
communication_framing: Lead with the user scenario and failure mode, then explain the interaction decision and how it can be evaluated.
preferred_vocabulary: user journey | task completion | interaction | feedback | error recovery | research | prototype
example_types: journey map | task-flow annotation | prototype state | research scenario
success_signal: Can identify an interaction decision, potential barrier, collaborator and research-based validation step.
avatar_attribution: RoboHash (https://robohash.org/), classic robot artwork by Zikri Kader

name: Visual Designer Val
summary: Val maintains a component library and wants visual accessibility decisions to survive implementation across states and environments.
scenario: Val designs components used by several teams. They need to specify focus appearance, type, spacing, contrast, responsive variants and adaptations to user preferences.
goals: Describe accessible visual states and component variants precisely. | Make accessibility annotations actionable in design handoffs. | Check rendered implementations rather than assuming design files demonstrate conformance.
needs: Visual comparisons of good and poor states. | Design-token, focus, colour, typography and reflow examples. | An explicit distinction between the design decision and implementation verification.
thoughts: Will the state remain clear when colours change or the layout reflows? | Have I specified enough for the developer to reproduce the intended behavior?
feelings: Frustrated when an accessible state is lost between the design and production. | Motivated by concrete examples that can be incorporated into the design system.
behaviors: Annotates component states and responsive variants. | Reviews the live interface with developers and compares it against design intent.
pain_points: Guidance that assumes a contrast check alone resolves all visual accessibility concerns. | Ambiguous handoffs for focus, hover, forced-colours and user preferences.
access_context: Sometimes reviews designs under variable lighting or altered contrast preferences; these situations do not define the role or a disability identity.
communication_framing: Use a visual state and its constraints first, followed by design specifications and what must be verified in the browser.
preferred_vocabulary: visual hierarchy | component state | focus indicator | contrast | typography | layout | design token
example_types: component variant | design token | state matrix | responsive annotation
success_signal: Can describe the expected visual outcome and coordinate verification with the implementing developer.
